input:
This case concerns the inventory policy for a resin grade, and specifically the level of safety stock that should be held to protect the cycle service level against variation in demand during the replenishment lead time. Demand for the grade averages 570 units per week, with a standard deviation of 99 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 2 weeks, so the exposure that the safety stock has to cover is the variation in demand that can accumulate over that lead time rather than over a single week. For a 95% cycle service level, the safety stock is 231 units. The figure rests on the assumptions built into the calculation: demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, which is what allows the weekly variation to be combined over the lead time in the way the calculation requires. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the treatment, and that exclusion matters in practice, because a policy sized on the stated demand pattern will not necessarily provide the same service level during a seasonal peak, when demand is systematically higher than the average pattern on which the safety stock figure was based. The stated figure therefore applies to the demand conditions described, and it should be revisited if the pattern of demand, or the lead time itself, changes.

The service level referred to is a cycle service level, which is to say the standard the policy sets for meeting demand during a replenishment cycle from stock, and the safety stock is the buffer that stands between ordinary variation in demand and a stock-out during the period in which a replenishment order is outstanding and cannot yet be drawn upon.
target:
Inventory policy for a resin grade sets safety stock at 231 units for a 95% cycle service level. Mean demand is 570 units per week, with a standard deviation of 99 units per week. Replenishment lead time is 2 weeks. Safety stock covers variation in demand over the lead time, not variation in a single week: demand fluctuations accumulate across the full period between ordering and delivery, and the stock must absorb the accumulated fluctuation if the service level is to be held. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks. The normal treatment sets the form of the calculation, and independence between weeks sets how weekly variation combines over the lead time. Seasonal peaks are excluded. A policy sized on the stated demand pattern does not necessarily give the same service level during a seasonal peak, when demand stands systematically above the average pattern. The safety stock figure applies to the demand conditions stated. A change in the pattern of demand, or in the lead time, changes the exposure the stock has to cover, and the figure is then set again from the new conditions.

The service level is a cycle service level: the standard set for meeting demand during a replenishment cycle from stock. Safety stock is the buffer between ordinary variation in demand and a stock-out during the period when a replenishment order is outstanding and cannot yet be drawn upon. Demand in some cycles exceeds the mean, and demand in others falls below the mean. The buffer is sized for the cycles in which demand runs high while delivery is still awaited.
